summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Flight disruptions expected to continue at UK airports today after technical issues
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
Flight disruptions at UK airports are expected to continue on Wednesday (September 9) due to a technical issue affecting air traffic control services. NATS, which provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports, was hit by the issue on Tuesday (September 8). As a result, around 1,300 flights to and from UK airports were cancelled, according to flight monitoring website Flightradar24. Tens of thousands of passengers were caught up in cancellations and delays. Further disruptions are expected on Wednesday as airlines deal with the knock-on effects at major UK airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted. Travel journalist Simon Calder warned that the effects on Wednesday were “going to be horrible”. Mr Calder told Sky News: “There are going to be dozens of cancellations in the morning of flights coming into Heathrow because, basically, the flights didn’t go out tonight.” Heathrow Airport said its operations were “still recovering” after the technical issue. Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew.
    Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be… pic.twitter.com/DZ2g7GQYkL — Heathrow Airport (@HeathrowAirport) September 9, 2026 Its website said: "Flights are operating today, however some knock-on disruption is expected as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. "Passengers are advised to check the latest status of their flight directly with their airline and to only travel to Heathrow if their flight is confirmed as operating today. "We apologise to passengers affected by the disruption. "Additional colleagues are available across our terminals to provide support, and we are working closely with NATS and our airline partners to return operations to normal as quickly as possible." Manchester Airport has said it is back "operating as normal" following Tuesday's technical issues. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), the airport added: "Those travelling today should continue with their journey plans and check with their airline for the latest information on their flight, as usual. “Thank you for your patience and understanding.” ℹ️ Information for passengers - 09.09.26 | 7:30am pic.twitter.com/y1jeR2VvRD — Manchester Airport (@manairport) September 9, 2026 Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted and that it had cancelled more than 50 scheduled flights as a result of NATS' technical issues. British Airways said it had been forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday, affecting “tens of thousands of customers”. Some passengers were trapped on planes on runways for hours. NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe said he “always accept(s) full responsibility” when asked whether he was considering his position after the incident. Mr Rolfe told Sky News: “I am the CEO of a piece of critical infrastructure, so it is my job to take responsibility for that.” “What I absolutely take responsibility for is keeping people safe and delivering the best service we possibly can on a day like today.” “You will understand my focus is entirely about how we actually resolve this issue, get things back to normal, help our airlines, our airport customers and the travelling public.” But Mr Rolfe has faced criticism from Wizz Air and Ryanair following the latest problem. Ryanair’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, called for Mr Rolfe to resign. Mr McMahon said: “How many more failures do passengers have to suffer before overpaid failure Nats CEO Martin Rolfe accepts responsibility for his repeated mismanagement and resigns?” “Over three years after Nats’ catastrophic 2023 system meltdown, it’s clear that nothing has changed, with UK passengers once again suffering avoidable ATC (air traffic control) delays of up to eight hours today due a critical Nats ATC system failing.” Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander is due to speak with Mr Rolfe on Wednesday. She is also expected to address MPs in the Commons during the second reading of the Civil Aviation Bill. NATS, posting on X on Tuesday night, said it will work on assisting airlines and airports recover from Tuesday’s technical issues. It added: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” “We apologise again for the disruption caused. Passengers should check with their airline on the status of their flight tonight or tomorrow.” ℹ️ Technical issue
    Work is continuing to assist airlines and airports recover from today's disruption. This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover. (1/2) https://t.co/Me6GAY385V — NATS (@NATS) September 8, 2026 Cancelled flights can leave passengers entitled to care, refunds, alternative travel and, in some cases, compensation, the UK Civil Aviation Authority explains. Under UK law, airlines must provide food and drink, a way to communicate, accommodation and transport when a flight is cancelled. This applies until passengers reach their destination, regardless of the delay’s length or its cause. If passengers need to stay overnight, airlines may arrange a nearby hotel and transport. Where an airline cannot provide care during major disruption, passengers can organise reasonable assistance themselves and claim the money back. Passengers should keep every receipt and avoid spending more than necessary. Passengers may also qualify for compensation if they received less than 14 days’ notice. This does not usually apply when cancellation was caused by extreme weather, airport or air traffic control strikes, or another extraordinary circumstance. For cancellations notified seven to 14 days ahead, compensation may be: This depends on the delay at the final destination, with lower amounts for shorter delays. For notice of less than seven days, passengers may claim £220, £350, £520 or £260, depending on flight distance and delay. Passengers can choose a refund for unused travel or an alternative flight. They may ask about another airline or suitable transport if it would get them there significantly sooner. Has your flight been affected by Tuesday's technical issues? Let us know in the poll above or in the comments below.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire Combined authority to review e-vehicle safety
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More children are reportedly suffering more head injuries after falling from scooters, a Cambridgeshire councillor has claimed. The claim has been made as concerns have been raised over a contract to provide e-bikes and scooters across parts of the county. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority currently has a contract with Voi to provide e-bikes and e-scooters across Cambridge and some surrounding areas. They were introduced as part of a trial in 2020 which has since been extended until May 2028. It is illegal to ride a privately owned e-scooter in public – only those offered by Voi as part of the trial can be legally used in the city. But some councillors have raised concerns over the vehicles blocking pavements, cluttering public spaces and the safety of riders. The combined authority’s overview and scrutiny panel asked for a report on the “social value” of e-scooters and data on injuries. Cllr Anna Bradnam, of South Cambs District Council, said they had also asked for data on illegal scooters and e-bikes too. She also asked for information to be provided by organisations that deal with head and brain injuries such as Headway and children’s hospices. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “Coincidentally, I have visited a hospice and just asked them out of the blue – because the hospice deals with children with life-limiting and life-changing conditions – have you seen more children come in because of falling off scooters? “They said, ‘oh, yes’ – I was really quite surprised, but of course lots of people on scooters don’t wear helmets.” Cllr Hugh Clough, of Cambridge City Council, said Voi had not consulted them before deciding where to put designated drop-off points. The Green councillor said: “Voi’s actual responsiveness to concerns raised by the public and councillors is a major issue in our area. “The lack of any sort of willingness to engage with councillors – that problem was raised too many times. “We’ve all got the list of problem sites where people can’t get through, can’t get in – you can’t even get your mobility scooter or wheelchair through. It’s a festering problem which needs to be addressed.” Cllr Bradnam asked for the topic to be brought to the panel as part of the January 2027 agenda list.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Police failures contributed to murder of mother-of-three, inquest finds
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have been heavily criticised for failing to protect a Biggleswade mother-of-three who was murdered by her partner. Sarah Albone, 38, was killed by her partner Matthew Waddell, 35, who was jailed for life in September 2023 for her murder. Her body was found in February 2023, three months after she was last seen, concealed in a suitcase inside a wheelie bin. Matthew Waddell murdered Sarah Albone and is serving life in prison. (Image: Bedfordshire Police) An inquest has found that police failures in recognising and responding to escalating domestic abuse contributed to her death. Police had been called to her home several times from August 2021. Senior coroner Emma Whitting found that Sarah faced such an immediate risk in the 16 months before her murder that the state had a duty to protect her, but had failed to do so. Waddell’s campaign of abuse began after meeting Sarah in November 2020. She had multiple sclerosis and became dependent on him, despite ending the relationship multiple times. Waddell repeatedly returned to her home and ignored police bail conditions. Sarah had reported him to police for harassment and assault, detailing his controlling and aggressive behaviour. Waddell killed her in a violent attack before hiding her body and sending messages from her phone to mislead friends and family. He was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 32 years. The case also triggered a Domestic Homicide Review, which identified failings across multiple agencies and called for a more trauma-informed approach to supporting vulnerable victims. A post-mortem examination found the cause of Sarah's death was airway obstruction due to catastrophic head injuries. It is believed she died in November 2022. John Tizard, police and crime commissioner for Bedfordshire, said: "My thoughts remain with Sarah’s family and all those affected by this deeply tragic case. "This case happened four years ago and systems and processes have changed but all agencies involved must accept their responsibilities, apologise, and learn the lessons. "The Domestic Homicide Review identified a number of failings across agencies, including missed opportunities to recognise vulnerability and a lack of vigilance in adopting a trauma-informed approach. "I shall be seeking assurances from the police and the Chief Constable that the failings identified four years ago could not arise in the same way today, and that and that every possible step has been taken to prevent such failings from occurring again."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire thieves who stole cars worth £500,000 feature in Channel 4 programme
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire thieves who stole cars worth £500,000 are featured in a Channel 4 programme. Three men from Peterborough—Osvaldas Milius, Mindaugas Savickas, and Kornelijus Girdeika—stole luxury vehicles worth more than £500,000 across Cambridgeshire in 2024. Their crimes featured on Channel 4’s 999: What Happened Next, which aired on September 7 at 9pm. The episode is now available to watch on demand. The trio were jailed for a combined nine years and 10 months in August last year. The gang stole 22 cars from Cambridgeshire and Lincolnshire between April and September 2024, including 16 Range Rovers, two Land Rover Discoverys, a Jaguar F-Pace, a BMW 118 and a Jaguar XF.

news.title: Fire service to finally withdraw after 'extremely tough' Holme Fen blaze
news.content: A major fire at a Cambridgeshire nature reserve that burned for more than a month is now under control. The blaze broke out at Holme Fen Nature Reserve in Cambridgeshire on August 8, leading to a major incident being declared by Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. More than 100 firefighters and 20 fire engines responded to the scene at its peak. The blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 (Image: Emily Stevens) After 31 days at the site, firefighters will hand control back to Natural England this week. Stuart Smith, assistant chief fire officer, said: "This has been the biggest incident our county has faced in many, many years. "We have seen crews from every fire station attend at some point during the response, as well as the fantastic support we’ve received from our colleagues across the country through National Resilience arrangements. "It’s been an extremely tough incident, especially with the gruelling hot weather we’ve seen over the last month or so, but we have reached a point where we feel it is safe for us to withdraw all crews and hand the site back over to Natural England." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Kimbolton Castle to glow for East Anglian Air Ambulance
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Kimbolton Castle will light up in support of a lifesaving charity. The historic site will glow red or yellow on Wednesday, September 9, in support of the East Anglian Air Ambulance (EAAA) as part of a wider display during Air Ambulance Week, helping raise awareness of the charity’s emergency care work across the region. Matthew Jones, CEO at East Anglian Air Ambulance, said: "We're incredibly grateful to Kimbolton Castle, Huntingdon Town Hall, Cromwell Museum and Godmanchester Chinese Bridge for supporting Air Ambulance Week and helping us raise awareness of the work our crews do every day. "Seeing well-known buildings illuminated across the region is a powerful reminder of the difference local communities make in helping us continue to provide lifesaving care, whenever and wherever it's needed." Other landmarks taking part include Peterborough Cathedral, the Guildhall/Corn Exchange and the Grand Arcade in Cambridge. The show of support comes as EAAA continues to fundraise for its Cambridge Air Base Appeal. The charity must relocate its operations ahead of Cambridge Airport's closure in 2030 and has so far raised £3.6 million towards the new base, with a further £4.4 million still needed. Mr Jones said: "This is about more than lighting up a building or making a donation – it's our community coming together to protect the people we love and secure the future of the lifesaving care we deliver across the counties we serve." Will Chuter, headteacher at Kimbolton School, said: "We're proud to support East Anglian Air Ambulance during Air Ambulance Week. "Lighting up Kimbolton Castle is a simple but meaningful way to recognise the dedication of the charity's crews and to encourage people to learn more about the incredible work they do across our community." Without the new Cambridge facility, EAAA's operations would be cut in half, with the replacement base planned for land at New Shardelowes Farm near Fulbourn.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fire service to finally withdraw after 'extremely tough' Holme Fen blaze
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major fire at a Cambridgeshire nature reserve that burned for more than a month is now under control. The blaze broke out at Holme Fen Nature Reserve in Cambridgeshire on August 8, leading to a major incident being declared by Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. More than 100 firefighters and 20 fire engines responded to the scene at its peak. The blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 (Image: Emily Stevens) After 31 days at the site, firefighters will hand control back to Natural England this week. Stuart Smith, assistant chief fire officer, said: "This has been the biggest incident our county has faced in many, many years. "We have seen crews from every fire station attend at some point during the response, as well as the fantastic support we’ve received from our colleagues across the country through National Resilience arrangements. "It’s been an extremely tough incident, especially with the gruelling hot weather we’ve seen over the last month or so, but we have reached a point where we feel it is safe for us to withdraw all crews and hand the site back over to Natural England." The fire spread around a four-kilometre perimeter, covering an area equivalent to around 60 football pitches, and burned deep into the peat. Firefighters from across the UK, including Durham and Darlington, Devon and Somerset, and Merseyside, were called in to assist. Crew Manager Jake Banks was called in to assist (Image: Emily Stevens) During the second week, around 50 firefighters worked on site by day and 30 overnight to control the blaze and clear the area. By the third week, the major incident had been stood down and National Resilience crews had returned home, leaving Cambridgeshire firefighters to clear the site and tackle hotspots. Mr Smith said: "We’ve had outstanding support from many people and places throughout the incident, which we are extremely grateful for. "It's not just the front-facing firefighters, the work behind the scenes to manage an incident like this is phenomenal. "Our own officers, control operators, and support colleagues ensured those on site had everything they needed and that we could maintain emergency cover across the county for other incidents, plus our neighbouring fire and rescue services have been incredibly supportive in helping with that too. The fire at Holme Fen has been burning for a month (Image: Sinead Everett) "Partner agencies, particularly the Environment Agency and Middle Level Commissioners, have played a major role in ensuring we had water supplies. "We've needed road closures, had ambulance colleagues on standby and worked closely with Natural England and contractors on site, who have worked so hard, to help us bring this fire to a safe conclusion as quickly as possible." He also praised local farmers, businesses and others in the surrounding community for supporting crews during the incident. Mr Smith said: "The Rapid Relief Team, The Admiral Wells pub, Ramsey Town Council, and everyone who has supported their efforts to provide food for firefighters at the scene has been at the heart of the community response. "Thank you doesn't seem enough, but we are so grateful for the support everyone has given." More than 40 firefighters tackled the blaze at Holme Fen (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service) He said a full review will now take place to inform future responses. Mr Smith said: "The next steps are just as important for us as a fire and rescue service. "In the coming weeks, we will undergo a thorough debrief process. "This was an unprecedented fire for us and it is important we take time to reflect and note what went well and highlight where we could improve should we have another incident like this again. "We do this for all larger incidents and it’s an invaluable process to ensure we continue to be as prepared as we can be for incidents and share that learning internally and nationally in the sector." Managed by Natural England, Holme Fen covers 657 acres and is designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest, supporting a wide variety of wildlife.

A woman in her 20s was arrested over the incident and released on bail. Anyone with information can email Detective Constable Lewis Stanley at Lewis.Stanley@herts.police.uk. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire rowing club is generating its own electricity after installing solar panels. St Neots Rowing Club is generating renewable electricity with a new solar and battery-storage system. The Warwick and Dominey Fund, administered by the Cambridgeshire Community Foundation, gave the club a grant for the project. The 34-panel system stores excess electricity in batteries for later use. It is expected to produce about 15,000kWh of electricity a year. That is enough energy to boil more than 500,000 kettles. Machelec designed and installed the system in three days, causing minimal disruption to the club’s activities. The club said the project is a major step towards long-term sustainability and could unlock further investment. It could also help the club switch from petrol to electric launches, cutting emissions, noise and pollution. The club also thanked member Lillian for helping make the solar panels a reality. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Reform councillor tables motion to stop further asylum accommodation in Hunts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A St Neots councillor will ask Huntingdonshire District Council to oppose any expansion of asylum accommodation and reject becoming a "Council of Sanctuary". Reform councillor Ricky Ioannides has tabled the motion for Wednesday’s full council meeting. The motion says immigration policy, asylum decisions and accommodation are matters for the Government and Home Office, but claims asylum housing can put pressure on homes, healthcare, policing and other local services. It states: "Huntingdonshire District Council does not consent to the further expansion of Home Office asylum accommodation within Huntingdonshire. "The council calls for an immediate moratorium on additional asylum accommodation capacity, for existing accommodation not to be renewed or replaced as contracts expire, and for the Home Office asylum accommodation estate within Huntingdonshire to be progressively reduced with the objective of ending its use within the district." If approved, the motion would put the council formally against any further expansion of Home Office asylum accommodation in Huntingdonshire. It would also say the district should not seek or support "Council of Sanctuary" status or anything similar. Councillors will be asked to back an immediate halt to any increase in asylum accommodation in the district. The proposal rules out new asylum hotels, more dispersed accommodation or additional homes, flats, HMOs and other premises for asylum use. The motion also calls on the Home Office and its contractors to let existing accommodation contracts expire without renewal or replacement, with the aim of ending asylum accommodation in Huntingdonshire. The council would not offer its land or property for asylum accommodation or promote Huntingdonshire as a site for future schemes. The motion also calls for the council to remove website wording saying it welcomes "asylum seekers, refugees and detainees" and replace it with politically neutral information on the roles of the council and Home Office. The motion also calls for regular reports to councillors on asylum property numbers and locations, the cost to council services and any expansion plans. The motion says it would not override the council’s legal duties, require unlawful discrimination or interfere with independent planning and regulatory decisions. If approved, the council’s executive leader would write to the Home Secretary, ministers, local MPs and Home Office accommodation providers to set out Huntingdonshire’s opposition to further expansion. National Home Office figures for June 2026 showed hotel placements had fallen by 50% year on year to 16,021, while dispersal accommodation increased by 4% to 69,038.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Plans for local government reorganisation in Cambs on hold as review launched
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Plans for local government reorganisation in Cambridgeshire are on hold due to new legal advice, the government has said. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said the review is to ensure the process is robust and aligns with the new Government’s aim to “rewire the state”, and follows “updated and privileged legal advice”. At least eight councils have launched legal challenges or were considering doing so due to opposition to the Government’s choice of footprints for new councils. Reform UK-led Kent County Council is set to consider a judicial review at a meeting on Tuesday after it did not receive a response from the Government to a letter setting out concerns. Plans for reorganisation in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn in the light of new legal advice. Decisions on 14 further areas will be reviewed and paused alongside the cases of Cambridgeshire & Peterborough and West Sussex, which are yet to have a decision confirmed. The Government will also confirm that local elections in May 2027 will go ahead on existing council boundaries, saying it remains committed to effective and sustainable local government and simplifying these structures. Communities Secretary Angela Rayner is expected to tell Parliament on Monday: “As we are now more determined than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent, it’s only right that as a new Secretary of State I make sure that everything we do is working towards that plan to change Britain, without delay. “The Prime Minister told the House last week he was ‘prepared to look at local government reorganisation’ and he asked me as his Communities Secretary to ‘do that’. “In that context, in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law. “And, secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new Prime Minister, and any additional considerations. “I do not take this lightly. I recognise the huge amount of work that has already gone into progressing reorganisation in each of these areas and I am very grateful for it.” MHCLG said reorganisation in Surrey will not be affected by the review and the two new unitary authorities, East and West Surrey, will go live in April 2027. Reform UK has claimed credit for the Government’s decision to halt the process, with the party leading county councils in Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex which all launched legal challenges to reorganisation. Reform leader Nigel Farage said: “Reform UK not only argued that this Government’s plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is. “Earlier this year we took on the Government and forced them to give the vote back to millions of people after Labour tried to cancel democracy. “Now, thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the Government has backed down on their plans yet again. “Only Reform had the backbone to stand up to these reckless plans. This is yet another embarrassing defeat for Labour. Only Reform backs real democracy.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Undercover investigation aired by Channel 4 a 'hoax', says Hunts Reform group
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Huntingdonshire Reform UK group has branded allegations over the party’s donations and vetting process a “hoax”. Two senior Reform officials stepped down on September 4 after Channel 4 aired an undercover investigation. Verbatim Investigations, founded by Centre for Climate Reporting journalists, filmed Nigel Farage and other Reform officials allegedly trying to bypass electoral law. Three influential opinion polls that made headlines for Reform before the May local elections were allegedly funded by a US company at the instruction of one of Mr Farage’s aides. However, the supposed donors behind the US company were actually undercover reporters. Footage shows Reform leader Mr Farage thanking the undercover reporters after the polls were published in May. Foreign donations are tightly regulated in the UK, and Mr Farage admitted to the BBC that the situation “looks bad”. Cllr Peter Gammons, of the Huntingdonshire Reform group, said: "Reform UK has been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. "The party denies any wrongdoing." Cllr Gammons said Reform was launching an internal investigation into the broadcast. He also questioned Verbatim Investigations’ credibility. Cllr Gammons said: "This is yet another establishment attack on Reform UK." The two officials were Reform's head of policy James Orr and long-serving Nigel Farage aide Dan Jukes. The Electoral Commission said it was considering all relevant information and had contacted the Metropolitan Police.

Residents have raised serious concerns about Huntingdonshire District Council’s draft Local Plan ahead of a key vote this week. More than 1,000 residents responded to a North Huntingdon & St Ives Cumulative Impacts Group survey, revealing widespread opposition to the plan’s evidence and proposed growth. More than 90 per cent said they did not trust the Local Plan’s evidence, while 93 per cent said it should not be finalised until clearer evidence was available. Around 60 per cent opposed the proposed growth, while 33 per cent backed development in principle but not at the draft’s scale. Only around 5 per cent supported the targets. Read more Reform councillor tables motion to stop further asylum accommodation in Hunts Further details emerge after police rush to Huntingdonshire bus station Structural concerns spark refusal of home plan for former meat preparation store 5 of the best-rated places in Cambridgeshire for a Sunday roast Hunts council motion to remove support from controversial car park plans Infrastructure was a major concern, with around 80 per cent worried about road congestion and almost 70 per cent concerned about water and wastewater capacity. Another 63 per cent highlighted pressure on schools and healthcare, along with the impact on the countryside and farmland. The survey closed as Huntingdonshire District Council’s overview and scrutiny panel for performance and growth met last week. Councillors reviewed the early findings and recommended that Cabinet and then Full Council consider the draft Local Plan on Wednesday (9). A survey carried out by the North Huntingdon & St Ives Cumulative Impacts Group attracted more than 1,000 responses from residents across the district and found widespread opposition to the evidence underpinning the plan and the scale of growth proposed. (Image: Huntingdonshire District Council) Officers acknowledge the widespread concern but are recommending approval for the plan, warning that delay or abandonment would restart the process and risk government intervention. A report says there are “no circumstances” to justify departing from the Government’s standard method for calculating housing need, so the overall requirement remains unchanged. Campaigners argue that the planning landscape changed after the new National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) was published in August 2026. The council can complete the plan under the previous framework, but campaigners say decisions made after adoption will be judged under the new national rules. The group also questions changes since earlier versions, including lower affordable-housing requirements, looser specialist and accessible-housing policies, a cut in self-build provision from five per cent to zero and biodiversity net gain reduced from 20 per cent to the statutory minimum of 10 per cent. Campaigners are particularly concerned about growth around Lodge Farm and Wyton Airfield, described in council documents as a “substantial new urban community”, according to the group’s statement. Campaigners say the council has not yet published a cumulative infrastructure assessment. Paul Boothman, chair of the North Huntingdon & St Ives Cumulative Impacts Group, said: "The survey shows overwhelming doubt in the evidence base and serious concern about infrastructure capacity. "Residents are asking councillors to look closely at these shortcomings and to test whether the plan is genuinely ready. "This decision cannot be made on assumptions - it needs clear answers." Campaigners say key questions remain over whether the plan will comply with the new national rules, whether infrastructure can keep pace, whether water-use assumptions are realistic and whether major growth areas have been assessed together. If full council approves it, the draft Local Plan will enter a six-week Regulation 19 consultation from mid-September to October, giving residents and organisations a final chance to make formal representations before examination by a planning inspector. The draft plan includes 24,000 homes, more than double the current housing stock in Huntingdon, which has about 10,000 homes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New 20mph limits in Cambridgeshire have reduced driver speeds, report shows
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A county council report revealed new 20mph limits on roads have shown “statistically significant” drops in speed a year after being introduced. Cambridgeshire County Council began introducing the new limits across the county from early 2024, across a total of 25 roads so far. The report, presented to the council’s highways and transport committee on Tuesday (September 1), looked at the impact of the limit on eight of these roads within the first year. It found that average speed was reduced on all of them. It looked at schemes in Cambourne, Histon, Ely, Great Abington, Fowlmere, Ramsey, St Neots, and Great Staughton. Speed reductions ranged from six per cent to 16 per cent, with the largest falls seen where speeds were highest before the limit was introduced. The report said early evidence of the limit’s impact on crashes is “encouraging but remains inconclusive” as numbers were already low in many towns. It said Ely is the only location which has so far shown a statistically significant fall in crashes, but Cambourne, Histon, and Ramsey have shown a downward trend. The report said there were an average of 15.6 crashes per year in Ely across the seven years from 2017, but this fell by nearly half in the scheme’s first year. It said there were eight crashes after the limit’s introduction, which was a “notable reduction” as crashes across Cambridgeshire had only fallen by 12 per cent. In St Neots, crashes actually increased during the first year but the report said this was not significant and falls within normal annual variation. It added that evaluating the scheme’s impact on crash rates will need at least three years of data, and recommended a further review at a later stage. The council collected anonymous data through sensors to determine speed and police road traffic collision records for crashes. The council has set aside £150,000 per year for new 20mph schemes with more currently planned or delivered in another 29 locations.

Plans to turn an agricultural building near Winwick into a four-bedroom home have been refused over structural concerns. Huntingdonshire District Council refused prior approval for the Bottom Farm scheme at The Green, Winwick, on September 3, and William Woodward submitted the application through agent David Hartley Associates. The scheme would have turned a former general store and meat-processing building into a detached home, with plans to add a first floor to the single-storey agricultural building and create a four-bedroom home. The building has about 107 square metres of floor space, while the proposed home would have 149 square metres. Plans to convert this agricultural building at a farm near Winwick into a four-bedroom home have been refused by Huntingdonshire District Council over concerns about the structure's ability to support the proposed development. (Image: David Hartley Associates/HDC) Planning officers agreed the building was part of an established agricultural unit and met many Class Q requirements. Those covered highway access, flood risk, contamination and natural light, and the county council’s highways team and the district council’s environmental health officers raised no objections. But officers said there was not enough structural evidence to support the proposed first floor. The report was based only on a visual inspection and contained no engineering calculations. Plans to convert this agricultural building at a farm near Winwick into a four-bedroom home have been refused by Huntingdonshire District Council over concerns about the structure's ability to support the proposed development. (Image: David Hartley Associates/HDC) It did not assess whether the existing steel frame and foundations could support the extra weight of the upper floor. The council’s officer report said: "The applicant has failed to provide adequate structural evidence demonstrating that the proposed first-floor accommodation can be accommodated within the existing building through works reasonably necessary to convert the building to residential use." The council said the evidence did not show the scheme was a straightforward conversion rather than substantial rebuilding. Read more NHS launches flu jab drive in Cambridgeshire and names who gets a free jab Cambridgeshire school term dates for 2026 and 2027 New 'school - keep clear' markings 'rubbing salt into wound' says councillor Ten people jailed across Cambridgeshire this month for crimes from rape to arson Inquest into death of 'beloved' Cambs mother who died unexpectedly at home The proposal therefore failed to meet Class Q permitted development rules, and the council refused prior approval. A structural assessment said the main barn was in good condition and suitable for conversion into a home. But it also said no monitoring, material testing or structural calculations had been carried out, and described it as a steel portal-framed barn thought to date from the mid-20th century. It said the barn was dry, weather-tight and free from significant distortion. Planning officers said the assessment did not examine the impact of adding a first floor or whether the building needed strengthening. Class Q rules allow agricultural buildings to become homes without a full planning application, subject to conditions and prior approval. The application was submitted on July 9, and no objections had been received by the time the council decided it. The council’s planning applications list also included a separate prior-approval application for a proposed pond at Valley Farm, Winwick.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Two Cambridgeshire businesses investigated over alleged underage sales
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two Cambridgeshire businesses are under investigation after allegedly selling age-restricted products to children. The alleged breaches were uncovered in undercover checks carried out over the summer by Cambridgeshire County Council Trading Standards, Volunteer Police Cadets aged 14 to 16, and city and district council licensing teams. The cadets tried to buy alcohol, vapes and tobacco from 26 premises flagged by complaints and intelligence. Peter Gell, head of Trading Standards at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "Selling these products to children can have serious impacts on their health and wellbeing. "Young people may not fully understand the long-term risks associated with using products such as tobacco and vapes at an early age. "Our work with partners to identify and take action against businesses that break the law will continue. "These exercises play an important role in protecting young people and ensuring retailers meet their legal responsibilities." Most businesses followed good practice, with staff checking the cadets’ ages and refusing to sell where appropriate. But two premises that sold age-restricted products to an underage cadet are now under investigation. Inspector Hayley Thind, from Prevention, Custody, and Partnerships at Cambridgeshire Constabulary, said: "The Volunteer Police Cadets promote good citizenship and have done a fantastic job in assisting our Trading Standards colleagues with this operation. "The cadets’ ongoing support of operations such as this is testament to their resilience and ability to work under pressure, so well done to them. "I am glad to see that the vast majority of local businesses complied with legislation and kept the young people in our communities safe." Trading Standards is encouraging retailers to review their age-verification policies and ensure staff consistently challenge anyone who appears under the age of 25. Mr Gell said: "With changes to legislation relating to tobacco and vape sales coming into force in the future, it is vital that businesses remain vigilant. "Retailers should ensure staff receive appropriate training, along with regular refresher training, and that robust procedures are in place to prevent underage sales." Concerns about young people getting alcohol can be reported to Cambridgeshire Police online. Report shops selling vapes or tobacco to under-18s to the Citizens Advice Consumer Service on 0808 223 1133 from Monday to Friday, or through its online form at weekends.

Huntingdonshire councillors will be asked to end the council’s involvement with car park regeneration proposals at a meeting this week. Councillor Ryan Coogan’s motion will be considered by the full Huntingdonshire District Council on Wednesday, September 9. Property developer Capital & Centric has proposed building housing developments on Tebbutts Road car park in St Neots, Princes Street bus station and car park in Huntingdon, and the former cattle market square and gatehouse in St Ives. The council's joint administration has already collapsed over the issue, with Green councillors quitting the Liberal Democrat-led coalition and citing the handling of the proposals. A consultation in Huntingdon drew a large turnout, with residents raising concerns about the potential loss of car parks in busy towns. The motion states: "Regeneration is important to the future prosperity of Huntingdonshire's towns. "However, regeneration involving public money and publicly owned assets must be founded upon clear objectives, a robust business case, demonstrable public benefit, value for money, proper scrutiny and meaningful engagement with the communities affected. "Members who previously supported progression of this work have subsequently expressed publicly that the proposals which emerged were not what they understood the Council had sought or expected from the process." If passed, the motion would confirm that the council does not support the projects going ahead. The council would also take steps to withdraw from the schemes and ask senior officers to review its relationship with Capital & Centric. Cllr Coogan will argue that residents should be able to “see clearly what public money was spent, what was commissioned, what was delivered”. The motion will be proposed at the full council meeting at 7pm on Wednesday at Pathfinder House, Huntingdon. Full details of the motion are on the Huntingdonshire District Council website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire primary school has welcomed a new robotic lawnmower after receiving a £1,500 donation to help maintain its playing field. Brington CofE Primary School received the high-tech mower thanks to a £1,500 donation from UK Power Networks. The mower, now named 'Mowli' following a naming competition, will help maintain the school field more efficiently, keeping it safe and tidy for pupils to use throughout the year. Mrs Baish, headteacher at Brington CofE Primary School, said: "We are incredibly grateful to UK Power Networks for their generous donation. "As a small school, every pound makes a real difference, and this funding has enabled us to make a positive investment that will benefit all of our children for years to come. "Our field is such an important part of school life, and we are delighted that Mowli will help us keep it looking its best." Year 2 pupil Madison came up with the winning name and received a £30 shopping voucher from UK Power Networks as a thank you for her idea. The donation is part of UK Power Networks’ commitment to supporting communities affected by its work. Andy Pearmain, project manager at UK Power Networks, said: "While the project has brought some disruption to the village, the team wanted to leave a positive legacy for the school and wider community. "We’re delighted that this donation will support Brington Primary and help the children continue to enjoy their school field for years to come." The school field is a central part of daily life at Brington, offering space for play, outdoor learning and sports. With Mowli now in action, the area can be maintained in a more efficient and sustainable way. Jimmy Ames, stakeholder engagement lead at UK Power Networks, said: "It’s fantastic to see the children getting involved and enjoying Mowli, while knowing that the donation will have a practical benefit for the school."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The 39 police dogs serving across Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire are receiving award-winning welfare support from a team of independent volunteers. Volunteers support the dogs through the BCH Independent Animal Welfare Visiting Scheme, run by the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner, across Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire. Dogs Trust awarded the scheme a Certificate of Compliance earlier this year for its high standards. The charity praised the scheme’s transparency, robust reporting and safeguarding of working dogs. The Commissioner said: "Our Animal Welfare Scheme is one of the many ways we provide accountability and transparency to the public. "Our police dogs make an invaluable contribution to policing across BCH. I would like to thank their handlers and the volunteers who give their time to independently monitor their welfare. Their work helps provide reassurance that our police dogs receive the care, support and protection they deserve." Scheme volunteers are trained to assess the dogs’ welfare and living conditions. Their independent visits give the public greater confidence in how the police dogs are treated. Inspector Stuart Carr, from the BCH dog unit, said: "Our Independent Dog Welfare Visitors play an important role in providing oversight of the care and wellbeing of police dogs across BCH. "These highly trained dogs support policing 24 hours a day, seven days a week, helping to keep our communities safe. "Police dog handlers hold a unique specialist role within the policing family, caring for their canine partners both on and off duty. "They are committed, dedicated and professional, with a deep respect and affection for the dogs they work alongside." The welfare scheme has run since 2012, reassuring the public and helping protect the dogs in its care. Across BCH, police dogs help search for missing people, locate suspects and recover evidence, alongside their wider role in keeping the public safe.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Festival marks 45th anniversary with big-screen celebrations
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridge Film Festival will celebrate its 45th anniversary this autumn with 11 days of international cinema, UK premieres and family favourites across the city. Running from October 22 to November 1, the festival will take place at Cambridge Arts Picturehouse and other venues, offering 11 days of international cinema, UK premieres and family favourites. Now one of the UK’s longest-running film festivals, it has earned BAFTA and BIFA qualifying status. Owen Baker, Cambridge Film Festival, said: "Forty-five years is a huge milestone. "We wanted to celebrate by doing what Cambridge Film Festival has always done best: bringing extraordinary films, filmmakers and audiences together and giving people something they won’t find anywhere else. "This year’s programme has real range and ambition. "We’ve got Palme d’Or and Cannes prize-winners alongside bold new British films, major international voices, brilliant documentaries and films that have already made an impact around the world. "There’s something for people who want to discover their next favourite film, and for those who simply want to come to the cinema and have a great time. "That feels like the right way to celebrate 45 years. "We’re proud of our history, but we’re also interested in where cinema is going next. "CFF45 is about taking that journey with our audiences; 11 days, films from around the world, new voices, familiar faces and plenty to discuss afterwards. "We can’t wait to open the doors." Nearly 100 titles from more than 25 countries will be featured, with over half directed by women, as marked by the festival’s F-Rating. Highlights include recent Cannes winners, major new works by established filmmakers, and a selection of films for younger audiences. The full programme will be available from September 30 on the festival’s website, www.camfilmfest.com, where tickets can also be booked. The festival is part of a year-long sapphire anniversary celebration, marking 45 years since its debut in 1977.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New Pulse Padel centre opens in Huntingdon as community hub
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Pulse Padel has officially opened its new padel facility at Blue Diamond Garden Centre in Huntingdon following a soft launch that drew interest from residents. The club is being billed as more than a set of courts — it aims to become a new community hub. The new facility offers padel courts for players of all ages and abilities The facility offers padel for players of all ages and abilities. Families can play together, while young people can build confidence, teamwork and resilience. Adults can stay fit while enjoying a social activity. Future plans include local leagues, inter-club tournaments, expanded coaching programmes, junior development pathways and specialist workshops. The opening comes as padel continues to grow in popularity across the UK The programme also includes coaching sessions for people with special educational needs and disabilities. The centre also plans community events, charity sessions and activities for schools. Plans also include launching Padel TV. The team is also hopeful for an alcohol licence to be granted soon, which would allow the centre to host social evenings, match day gatherings, and community celebrations. The team has been praised for its vision, dedication and passion in creating the facility. Pulse Padel aims to provide a new sporting and social hub for the local community The centre aims to become a hub for activity, wellbeing and community connections. The opening comes as padel grows in popularity across the UK. The Huntingdon centre plans to host coaching sessions, leagues and community events Huntingdon residents now have a new way to stay active. The team says the centre’s early success reflects its hard work and the community spirit behind the project. Pulse Padel has submitted a retrospective planning application to retain the three courts and associated facilities at the garden centre. The application covers a 980-square-metre site, including a cabin with changing facilities, reception, customer amenities and a small refreshment area. If approved, the proposed opening hours would be 7am to 11pm from Monday to Saturday and 8am to 10pm on Sundays and bank holidays.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Police commissioner praises charity volunteers who support victims of road tragedies
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Police and Crime Commissioner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough has praised the work of volunteers who support victims of road tragedies. Darryl Preston commended the dedication of those who volunteer with the Road Victims Trust (RVT), a charity providing emotional and practical support to people affected by road collisions. Mr Preston said: "The value of specialist counselling in such tragic and devastating circumstances cannot be underestimated." The trust offers long-term, confidential counselling and support to bereaved families, witnesses and individuals directly involved in road incidents. Services are delivered free of charge and tailored to each person's needs. The PCC has committed £70,000 in funding for the charity in 2026/27. In 2025/26, 17 volunteer counsellors donated more than 1,200 hours of support in Cambridgeshire, tripling the value of the funding through an estimated £120,000 of additional support. Mr Preston said: "Over the years, RVT staff and volunteers have helped to rebuild thousands of lives and provide hope for those affected by the trauma of road tragedy. "When the very worst happens, it is heartening to know the RVT is available to ensure victims do not suffer alone. "There are experienced counsellors who help people find the tools and the courage to rebuild their lives." Paul Cook, CEO of the Road Victims Trust, also highlighted the importance of the service. Mr Cook said: "National Road Victim Month is an important opportunity to remember every person whose life has been changed by a road collision and to recognise the compassion and commitment of those who support them. "We are extremely grateful for the commissioner’s continued support and for the dedication of our trained volunteer counsellors, who give their time and expertise to ensure that people do not have to face the devastating consequences of a road collision alone."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Heritage Open Day to shine spotlight on Alconbury's military past
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Dakota flypast and a day of history and celebration are planned for a heritage event in Huntingdonshire. The annual Heritage Open Day, taking place at Alconbury Weald, will be held on Saturday, September 12, from midday to 5pm. This year’s event will shine a spotlight on Alconbury’s military past, featuring an exhibition of artefacts from its World War II and Cold War-era buildings. Natalie Leigh-Brown, senior community development lead at Alconbury Weald, said: "Alconbury Weald has an amazing heritage dating back to early Bronze Age settlers and it’s a privilege to be able to share some of it at our Heritage Open Days. Alconbury Weald celebrates rich heritage with community fun day (Image: TIM GEORGE) "This year, we’re focusing on its more recent military past and the role Alconbury Airfield played in World War II and the Cold War. "The Community Association’s Family Fun Day running alongside ensures a great mix of culture and entertainment for residents and visitors, with lots for all ages and interests to enjoy." A talk from the Airfield Research Group will take place at 3pm, and pre-booked tours of the Cold War Avionics Building are already fully booked. Heritage Open Day explores Alconbury Weald’s military past (Image: TIM GEORGE) One of the day’s highlights will be a Dakota flypast by the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight, scheduled for the afternoon, weather permitting. The event is part of Heritage Open Days, England’s largest festival on history and culture. Alconbury Weald Community Association will also host a Family Fun Day alongside the heritage activities. History and family fun combine at Alconbury Weald (Image: TIM GEORGE) Visitors can enjoy food trucks, Pimms, scones, face painting, live music, and more. Entry to the event is free, and most activities are available on a drop-in basis. Residents are encouraged to walk or cycle, while visitors can use the AW1 or 904 bus services to The Boulevard stop. Free parking will be available behind The Incubators, with signage provided on the day.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Business leaders welcome government support for small firms
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire business leaders have welcomed a government commitment to helping small firms grow following talks with the Minister for Small Business and Enterprise. The Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce voiced its support following a recent meeting with Lord Leong CBE, Minister for Small Business and Enterprise. Charlotte Horobin, CEO of Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "It was a real pleasure to meet Lord Leong and discuss how we can work together to unlock growth for small businesses across our region and beyond. "Small businesses are the backbone of our economy, and they need the right support, skills, connections and opportunities to realise their full potential." During the meeting, chamber representatives highlighted the ongoing challenges facing businesses in the region, including rising employment costs, tariffs, and economic uncertainty. The conversation focused on digital adoption, export growth, and the development of skills, jobs, and apprenticeships. Charlotte said: "There is a huge amount of ambition among businesses across Cambridgeshire, and we look forward to working with Lord Leong and the Government to ensure that ambition translates into investment, exports, innovation, jobs and apprenticeships." The chamber is already supporting businesses with initiatives such as its AI Academy, a trade mission to Azerbaijan, PROJECT Fairfax, and the Local Skills Improvement Plan. Charlotte also emphasised the value of the chamber’s Quarterly Economic Survey (QES), which gathers business insights to inform national policy. She said: "Our Quarterly Economic Survey also gives us a powerful way to bring the voice of local businesses directly into the national conversation. "For us, that means our role goes beyond providing services to individual businesses. "We can take the collective voice of thousands of businesses and use it to inform policy and make the case for the conditions they need to grow." The chamber said it looks forward to welcoming Lord Leong to Cambridgeshire in the future and continuing its work with government and regional partners.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Swan on tracks causing disruption as passengers warned of delays
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Passengers have been warned of delays after reports of a swan on the tracks. Some lines are blocked after the bird made it onto the line between Peterborough and Stevenage at around 9am on Saturday (September 5). Commuters are being advised to allow at least an additional 60 minutes to complete journeys amid warnings trains may be delayed or revised. Disruption is expected until at least 10.30am, National Rail confirmed. A spokesperson said: "We have been advised of a swan on the track in the Peterborough area. "In this case, as we aren't allowed to deliberately cause any harm to the swan, trains will run at reduced speeds. "In addition, if the swan is found to be obstructing trains, services will need to stop on approach. This will lead to further delays. "Network Rail's response staff are attending as quickly as possible to make sure the swan is removed and the railway is as secure as possible." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: What to expect at the Sandringham Country Fair 2026
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Organisers of The Sandringham Game and Country Fair say the event will be full of entertainment and displays to keep families entertained all day long. The fair will take place on September 12 and 13, from 10am to 6pm. Attendees can look forward to a variety of high-speed equestrian events such as scurry driving and horse boarding, where riders race against the clock through an obstacle course. The main show arenas will also feature falconry, stunt teams, gun dog demonstrations, fly casting, and wildfowling. The 'Food Glorious Food' section promises a feast for the senses with food halls, cookery demonstrations, street food, bars, and live music. The Sandringham Game and Country Fair is full of entertainment and displays (Image: Sandringham Game & Country Fair) Craft enthusiasts can explore marquees filled with artists, designers, jewellers, potters, and wood turners, alongside traditional craft demonstrations like glass blowing and blacksmithing. Adventure seekers can participate in 'have-a-go' events including airguns, archery, clay shooting, fishing, and a range of dog events. A spectacle of steam engines, stationary engines, tractors, vintage cars, military vehicles, funfair rides, and puppet shows will also be on display. Tickets can be booked online at www.livingheritagecountryshows.com/tickets or by calling 01283 82.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts family is raising cash and awareness of womb cancer in memory of mum
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdon family is organising a charity karaoke night in memory of her mum, who died just 11 days after being diagnosed with womb cancer earlier this year. Kara Howarth, 24, is planning the event in honour of her mum Tina, who was 53 when she was diagnosed with endometrial cancer on March 28 this year. Tina sadly died on April 8. The fundraiser will take place at the Waggon and Horses pub in St Neots on October 2 from 7pm. It will raise money for PEACHES Womb Cancer Trust while helping to spread awareness of womb cancer and its warning signs. Tina Howarth pictured with Kara and Angel. (Image: Kara Howarth) Kara said: “Losing my mum has taught me that life can be so short, so we should spend a little less time worrying and more time having fun. “While the main purpose is to raise money and awareness for endometrial cancer in support of PEACHES Womb Cancer Trust, I really want it to be a night full of fun, laughter and memories — a reminder to enjoy life to the absolute full.” She is being helped with the event by her dad, Richard, from Huntingdon, and her older sister Angel, who lives in Leeds. Tina Howarth's favourite picture of her and her girls, a copy of the photo, was put inside her coffin with her. (Image: Kara Howarth) Kara said she had been overwhelmed by the support already received after the £1,000 target on her JustGiving page was reached in less than 48 hours. She hopes donations will continue, with funds going towards research into womb cancer and support for people affected by it. Kara said: “We lost Mum, but we haven’t lost her fight. “So we’ll keep making noise. We’ll keep raising awareness. We’ll keep fighting for change. And in true karaoke fashion, we’ll do it loudly.” Tina Howarth, and her husband Richard pictured at Kara's graduation day last year. (Image: Kara Howarth) PEACHES Womb Cancer Trust supports patients and families, funds and promotes research, and works to increase public awareness of the disease. Womb cancer, also known as endometrial cancer, is the UK’s most common gynaecological cancer and affects around 10,000 women each year. Most people diagnosed are over 50 and have been through the menopause, although it can also affect younger women. A survey commissioned by PEACHES found that around one in five UK women had never heard of womb cancer. Kara said her mum had been among those unaware of the disease before becoming ill. “My mission is to raise awareness and raise money towards helping others and researching womb cancer and how we can improve the care, the diagnosis and the treatments available for women, so that women and families do not have to go through what my mum and my family went through,” she said. Tina Howarth on her wedding day with husband Richard. (Image: Kara Howarth) The main warning sign is unusual vaginal bleeding. This includes any bleeding after the menopause, as well as heavier periods than usual, bleeding between periods or after sex, and unusual discharge. Other possible symptoms include persistent lower tummy pain, bloating, blood in urine and unexplained weight loss. Tina Howarth's daughter Kara is holding a karaoke evening in her memory to raise awareness of womb cancer. (Image: Kara Howarth) Tina Howarth pictured at Burghley one of her favourite places. (Image: Kara Howarth) Tina Howarth pictured with Kara when she was a little girl. (Image: Kara Howarth) Tina Howarth and her daughters in happy times. (Image: Kara Howarth) Kara said her mum had believed her bleeding was part of the menopause. She urged women to get any unusual bleeding checked as quickly as possible, stressing that bleeding after menopause is not normal.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Do not eat' warning issued to Tesco shoppers after 'health risk' recall
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Tesco is warning shoppers not to eat one of its products which has been recalled due to a potential health risk. The supermarket giant is recalling the Tesco Finest Caesar & Smoked Bacon Coleslaw due to a packaging error. The mistake means that some packs may actually contain Tesco Finest Four Cheese Potato Salad, meaning that it also contains mustard not declared on the label. As a result, it is a possible health hazard for anyone with an allergy to mustard. Wednesday 3rd September - Tesco recalls Tesco Finest Caesar & Smoked Bacon Coleslaw because of undeclared mustard #FoodAllergy https://t.co/JRHL6RKA7q pic.twitter.com/YU0gMmSKs2 — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) September 3, 2026 The affected coleslaw comes in 270g packets and has a use by date of September 4. A spokesman for the Food Standards Agency said: “Tesco is recalling the above product from customers and has contacted the relevant allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall. “The company has also issued a recall notice to its customers. These notices explain to customers why the product is being recalled and tell them what to do if they have bought the product. “If you have bought the above product and have an allergy to mustard do not eat it. Instead return it to any Tesco store for a full refund. “For further details, please visit the contact page of Tesco's website: tesco.com/help/contact.” Tesco added: “If you’ve bought the affected product and have an allergy to mustard, please don’t eat. “Instead, return the product to any Tesco store where a full refund will be given. No receipt is required. “No other Tesco products are affected by this recall. We’re sorry for any inconvenience caused.” If there is a problem with a food product that means it should not be sold, then it might be 'withdrawn' (taken off the shelves) or 'recalled' (when customers are asked to return the product). The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. In some cases, a 'Food Alert for Action' is issued. This provides local authorities with details of specific actions to be taken on behalf of consumers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: State Pension age rises to 67 - who will be hit hardest as age goes up?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of people are facing a longer wait for their State Pension, but some could be hit much harder than others. The State Pension age is rising from 66 to 67, with the change being phased in between April 2026 and April 2028. For someone who is healthy and able to remain in work, waiting longer may be manageable. But for others, those extra months could create a serious financial gap, particularly if they have little savings and are unable to continue working. A tax expert has warned that seven groups could be particularly vulnerable as the new State Pension age takes effect. The Work and Pensions Committee has previously warned that the impact of the increase is unlikely to be felt equally across the country. Andy Wood, a tax expert at Tax Barrister UK, said: “The increase means that affected individuals will have to wait longer before becoming eligible for their State Pension. “For those who are healthy, in secure employment and able to continue working, that additional wait may be manageable. "However, it could create a serious financial gap for people who cannot remain in work and do not have sufficient savings or other assets to support themselves.” The groups identified as particularly vulnerable include: These circumstances can overlap, potentially leaving some people facing several financial pressures at once. Someone who has spent years in a physically demanding, lower-paid job, for example, may also have caring responsibilities or health problems that make it difficult to work until their new State Pension age. Wood said: “These circumstances frequently overlap. Someone may have worked in a lower-paid or physically demanding job while also having caring responsibilities or experiencing health problems. “This can make it more difficult to build private pension savings, accumulate other assets or continue working until the new State Pension age. “People approaching retirement should therefore check their expected State Pension age and forecast rather than assuming they will automatically become eligible when they turn 66.” Recommended reading: The rise from 66 to 67 is not happening overnight. It is being introduced gradually, meaning the exact date someone becomes eligible depends on their date of birth. People born between 6 April 1960 and 5 March 1961 will reach State Pension age at 66 plus a specified number of months. For example, someone born on 31 July 1960 is expected to reach State Pension age at 66 years and four months. This means people approaching retirement should not simply assume that turning 66 means their State Pension will start. Wood said: “The exact date on which someone becomes eligible will depend on their date of birth. It is important to check this directly through the Government’s State Pension age service, particularly when making retirement or employment plans. “People should also check their National Insurance record and State Pension forecast. Reaching State Pension age does not necessarily mean everyone will receive the same amount, as entitlement will depend on an individual’s National Insurance history.” For someone unable to continue working, the wait for their State Pension could mean relying on other sources of income for longer. That could include working-age benefits or savings that had originally been earmarked for retirement. The Work and Pensions Committee has highlighted concerns about the potential impact on people who cannot remain in employment until their State Pension age. Previous evidence also indicated that when the State Pension age increased from 65 to 66, the absolute poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled. Wood said: “A delay of several months may sound relatively small, but it could represent a considerable loss of expected income for someone who has already left work. “Those without substantial savings may need to rely on Universal Credit or other available support until they qualify for their State Pension. Others could be forced to use retirement savings earlier than planned. “The change may be particularly difficult for people in physically demanding roles or those with medical conditions that limit the type or amount of work they can undertake.” The committee has called on the Government to consider increasing Universal Credit payments for 66-year-olds affected by the transition. The changes do not stop at 67. Under current legislation, the State Pension age is due to rise again from 67 to 68 between 2044 and 2046. However, that timetable could still change following future Government reviews. For anyone approaching retirement, the key point is that their State Pension age is determined by their date of birth, rather than simply reaching their 66th birthday. Checking the Government's State Pension age service, National Insurance record and State Pension forecast could help people understand when they are likely to qualify and how much they may receive. For those unable to continue working and without significant savings, knowing the date in advance could be particularly important when planning how to bridge the gap before State Pension payments begin.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare warbird forced to make a belly landing after engine issue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare warbird was forced to make a belly landing after suffering an engine issue during a maintenance check flight. The Fighter Collection's Curtiss P-40C Warhawk G-CIIO came down northwest of Royston on August 25 after taking off from IWM Duxford, in Cambridgeshire. The aircraft suffered an engine issue during a maintenance check flight which forced the pilot to perform a wheels up landing. The pilot evacuated unaided and directed the Duxford Fire & Rescue Team to the scene. The Fighter Collection said: "We are indebted to the IWM security team for providing mobile security units to the site ensuring the safety of the aircraft whilst the engineering team dismantled the aircraft." Highfield Farm staff helped lift the aircraft on to its landing gear before it was towed to safety. The Fighter Collection added: "We are further indebted to the Welch's Specialist Movements team who provided the logistics and highways permits to repatriate the airframe back to hangar T2S today." The Curtiss P-40C Warhawk served with several Allied air forces during the Second World War and was America’s third most-produced fighter of the conflict. The aircraft is rare in the UK, with G-CIIO one of only three airworthy examples before last week’s incident.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Miniature railway plans submitted for Huntingdonshire community nursery site
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A planning application has been lodged for a miniature railway at a Godmanchester Community Nursery after council enforcement officers halted work the project. The plan would put the railway along the eastern and northern edges of the five-acre, volunteer-run Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery on Park Lane, which includes a community orchard, with the aim of adding an attraction for families. A design, access, and heritage statement submitted alongside the application says work had begun on the railway track base before Huntingdonshire District Council enforcement officers stopped it, and the application seeks permission for the work already done and to finish the railway. Harry Quenault submitted the scheme for Godmanchester Town Council, with planning agent Chris McCrae acting for the applicant; the application describes it as the "installation of a miniature railway". Eye level image of the existing track installation adjacent to the southern 'platform 1', demonstrating its low impact on the land. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The statement says the railway would attract visitors while keeping rides affordable at £1, and supporters say it would offer families a cheap activity, encourage repeat visits and improve access to the site’s rare apple orchard. The design and heritage statement says the railway would complement, not replace, the nursery’s role as a community resource. It states: "The proposal is not to turn the site into a theme park. It is to add a modest attraction that complements horticulture, outdoor activity and community access." The document also points to Godmanchester’s railway heritage through the former Huntingdon to St Ives line, and planners say the attraction could introduce younger generations to the area’s railway history and draw more visitors. Eye level image traveling toward the northern end of the site, illustrating the track base prepared to receive the track prior to enforcement notice. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The railway would run mostly at ground level, with two platforms, a turntable at the northern end and a low timber fence around the track, and planning documents say the route is designed to minimise its impact on the orchard and neighbouring properties. The site is in a flood-risk area, but the applicant says the project qualifies as minor development and would not increase the risk, while the documents say the track would sit on maintained grassland and would not reduce biodiversity. If approved, the railway would run during fair-weather events only, from 10am to 3pm, Tuesday to Saturday. Aerial view of the site from the west looking towards the eastern boundary. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The design and access statement adds: "The purpose of the proposed Godmanchester Miniature Railway at the Community Plant Nursery is not simply to introduce a visitor attraction. It is to make an existing community-facing site work harder." Huntingdonshire District Council will decide the application later. Aerial view of the north-east corner of the site, and the relationship between the track and the eastern boundary and properties/community orchard beyond. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) At the nursery's Apple Day in October 2025, train rides provided by the Sawtry Miniature Railways Group doubled the team's previous daily record of 200 rides.
